claims.text: Sub-10 nm FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles undergo surface premelting at lower temperatures than 20–30 nm particles.
Sub-10 nm FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles completely melt at lower temperatures than 20–30 nm particles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio and higher surface curvature.
Higher curvature modifies surface atomic coordination and internal stress in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
A larger fraction of surface atoms and higher curvature decrease the effective cohesive energy of smaller nanoparticles.
Reduced effective cohesive energy lowers the energy barrier for melting.
Earlier surface premelting accelerates propagation of the liquid phase through smaller nanoparticles.
Compositionally uniform FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles can be prepared as distinct sub-10 nm and 20–30 nm populations.
The two size populations can be made highly monodisperse without changing nominal composition.
All synthesis parameters other than nanoparticle size can be held constant between the two populations.
In situ synchrotron XRD and TEM can capture the onset and progression of melting under an inert-atmosphere thermal ramp.
A broad, unseparated size distribution has an average phase-transition onset representative of that distribution.
The proposed size-dependent mechanism applies to solid, compositionally homogeneous, highly monodisperse FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles heated under inert conditions.
High polydispersity, interparticle interactions, or external coatings may alter or obscure the proposed size-dependent thermal behavior.
The qualitative trend of size-dependent melting is well established for nanoparticles.
Residual polydispersity and variations in synthesis and measurement conditions may change the magnitude of the observed temperature shift.
No statistically significant difference in melting onset or melting kinetics between the two size classes would falsify the claim that size-dependent surface effects dominate melting.
